name: CKTSO-GPU
language: C++ (CUDA; solver shipped as prebuilt x86-64 Windows/Linux binaries, demos in C++)
baseline: KLU 1.3.9 (SuiteSparse; run with CKTSO's ordering); also CKTSO version 20221123 on 1 CPU thread
workload: Sparse LU re-factorization time and forward/backward solve time for 29 SuiteSparse circuit matrices with Flops/NZ(L+U) > 50, on an RTX 3090 versus single-thread CPU CKTSO and sequential KLU.
claimed_speedup: Re-factorization: CKTSO-GPU is 28.80X (arithmetic mean) / 13.29X (geometric mean) faster than KLU and 12.01X / 6.11X faster than CKTSO (1 thread). Solving: 2.41X / 1.72X faster than KLU and 1.98X / 1.46X faster than CKTSO (1 thread). Per-matrix times appear only as bar charts.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.5 and nvcc 11.0 on CentOS 7.9.2009 x64 (optimization flags not stated); 32-bit integer interface
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6130 (16 cores, 2.1 GHz), NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 (24 GB), 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Closed-source: the repo ships only prebuilt x86-64 libraries (libcktsogpu.so, cktsogpu.dll, plus _l 64-bit-integer variants), a header, and demo sources; it also needs the CKTSO library and its cktso.lic from the sibling repo. NVIDIA/CUDA only. Per its own user guide it only helps slightly-dense circuit matrices (recommended when flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50) and cannot efficiently accelerate highly sparse circuit matrices; plain multicore CKTSO is best for those. One right-hand side per solve call. Pivoting factorization still runs on the CPU; only re-factorization and solve run on the GPU.
caveats: First-party results.pdf (version 20221207) only; no benchmark code is public and the solver source is not available, so this cannot be rerun. The GPU is compared only with CKTSO on ONE thread and with sequential KLU, not with multithreaded CKTSO, NICSLU, cuSOLVER or GLU, so the speedup is partly a GPU-vs-one-core comparison. The 29 matrices were selected for high Flops/NZ(L+U) (> 50), which favours the GPU. KLU is given CKTSO's ordering. Whether host-device transfers are included in the GPU times is not stated. A readme in the repo's disabledL1cache folder says some GPUs (V100 named) give wrong results unless L1 cache is disabled, at about 20% performance loss. No license text in the repo (reference only). Repo last updated 2023-04-01. Dates of last commit were read from the GitHub commits page.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/chenxm1986/cktso-gpu (results.pdf and ug.pdf in the repo)

name: NICSLU
workload: Sparse LU solving of 182 circuit matrices (136 from real circuits, 46 from SuiteSparse); the page's performance chart is labelled normalized refactor+solving time (NICSLU = 1), with companion charts for fill-ins and pre-analysis time; all solvers use 'best configurations'.
claimed_speedup: NICSLU achieves 2.15X speedup over Intel MKL PARDISO and 1.87X speedup over KLU, both on geometric mean over the 182 matrices; faster than KLU on 149 of 182 cases (82%) and faster than MKL PARDISO on 134 of 182 (74%). Fewer fill-ins: KLU generates 29.6% more and PARDISO 46.1% more than NICSLU (geometric mean). Pre-analysis is slower: KLU spends 61% less pre-analysis time than NICSLU, while NICSLU spends 54% less than PARDISO.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in results.pdf. Prebuilt libraries in the repo are named lib_centos6_x64_gcc482_fma / _no_fma (gcc 4.8.2, CentOS 6); flags unknown.
hardware: Intel Gold 6132 CPU (core/thread count not stated); NICSLU version 201905B
tradeoffs: Proprietary and binary-only: nicslu202110 holds Linux and Windows libraries (FMA and non-FMA builds), a license key file nicslu.lic, demos and docs, but no solver source. Per ug202110.pdf it is copyrighted by NICS Laboratory (Tsinghua) and Xiaoming Chen, protected by three Chinese patents, free for academic use and 'distributed for customization or research'; commercial use requires contacting the authors. The license key file is readme-marked for research/trial use and the key was extended to 9999-99-99. Author states it is no longer maintained and points to the successor CKTSO. Shared-memory multicore only.
caveats: First-party 2019 results.pdf (NICSLU 201905B, newer 202110 libraries were published afterwards). No benchmark code and no source, so it cannot be rerun; 136 of the 182 matrices are real circuit cases that are not public. Compiler, flags and thread counts for any solver are unstated, and 'best configurations' is not defined. KLU is a sequential solver. The user guide cites peer-reviewed papers (IEEE TCAD 2013 vol. 32 no. 2 pp. 261-274 'NICSLU: An Adaptive Sparse Matrix Solver for Parallel Circuit Simulation'; DATE 2015, 2016; Springer book 2017) that I could not open (IEEE and publishers are egress-blocked), so the tier stays C. Author says CKTSO (already on the known list) supersedes it. Last commit date is from the GitHub commits page (March 2026 'Final update').

name: DASP (dense-tensor-core SpMV)
baseline: cuSPARSE CSR SpMV (CUSPARSE_SPMV_ALG_DEFAULT); also CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR and cuSPARSE BSR in the paper
workload: General sparse matrix-vector multiplication (y = Ax) on SuiteSparse matrices in FP64 and FP16 on NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs, using tensor-core MMA units; the repo's harness times cuSPARSE and DASP for 1000 iterations after 100 warm-ups for a given .mtx file.
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'23) FP64 on A100: DASP outperforms CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR, cuSPARSE BSR and cuSPARSE CSR by a factor of on average 1.46x, 2.09x, 3.29x, 2.08x and 1.52x (up to 12.64x, 17.48x, 90.59x, 283.92x and 6.94x), respectively. FP16 versus cuSPARSE: on average 1.70x and 1.75x (up to 26.47x and 65.94x) on A100 and H800. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text for the paper; see caveats.)
compiler_and_flags: From the repo Makefile: nvcc from CUDA 12.0 with host gcc 12.2, -O3 -m64 -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80, -Xcompiler -fopenmp-simd, linked with -lcusparse -lcublas
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs (per the paper text returned by search); the repo recommends a GPU with compute capability 8.0. Host CPU model not verified.
tradeoffs: Needs NVIDIA GPUs with MMA tensor-core support (compute capability 8.0 or newer; FP64 and FP16 variants built from separate mains: make double, make half). Research code driven by Matrix Market files, not a library API. Rows are grouped into long, medium and short categories and repacked into MMA-sized blocks, which adds preprocessing and padding (fill-zero) data. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies to anything built on the code.
caveats: The paper PDF could not be opened (dl.acm.org, ssslab.cn and other publishers are egress-blocked here); the benchmark_url was returned by WebSearch and the speedup numbers above come from that result's text (abstract-level, 'snippet only'), including the A100-only list of averages. The repo itself holds no result tables; I read its harness (src/main_f64.cu, src/dasp_f64.h): it times only the SpMV kernels, and the DASP row reordering / format conversion is not part of the timed loop (cuSPARSE buffer setup is also timed separately), so gains only pay off when the same matrix is multiplied many times. The repo has no scripts for the CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR or BSR baselines, so only the cuSPARSE comparison is reproducible from the repo. cuSPARSE version used in the paper is not verified. Could move to tier A if the paper's setup table lists CPU model and library versions. Large 'up to' ratios (283.92x vs BSR) are outliers; averages are the meaningful figures.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/DASP and one WebSearch query for the SC'23 paper numbers

name: TileSpMV
baseline: cuSPARSE, CSR5 and merge-based SpMV (per the task lead; the exact baselines and ratios could not be verified)
workload: SpMV on GPUs over the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection using 16x16 sparse tiles with seven warp-level kernels (CSR, COO, ELL, HYB, dense, dense row, dense column) and per-tile format selection; paper is IPDPS 2021.
claimed_speedup: No numbers available to me. A WebSearch result summary says only that TileSpMV 'is faster than state-of-the-art SpMV methods in most matrices of the full SuiteSparse Matrix Collection'. The repo README has no performance numbers.
compiler_and_flags: From src/Makefile: nvcc, CUDA 11.1 path, -O3 -w -arch=compute_61 -code=sm_86 -gencode=arch=compute_61,code=sm_86, -Xcompiler -fopenmp -O3, MAT_VAL_TYPE=double
hardware: README: NVIDIA Tesla K40 'as tested', CUDA 11.1, Ubuntu 18.04/20.04; paper hardware not verified
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPUs only (compute capability 3.5 or newer). Matrices are first converted to a tiled format (csr2tile), and very sparse tiles are split into a separate matrix; conversion cost and the extra format memory are tradeoffs. Research code driven by a Matrix Market file (./test -d 0 matrix.mtx). Bundles the CSR5 CUDA code under src/external/CSR5_cuda.
caveats: Evidence is a peer-reviewed IPDPS 2021 paper (Niu, Lu, Dong, Jin, Liu, Tan, pp. 68-78) whose full text and abstract numbers I could not open (IEEE, ACM, Semantic Scholar and ResearchGate are egress-blocked; the single WebSearch snippet had no ratios), so I record no speedup and tier D. A verifier with paper access could likely re-tier to B. The repo's src/main.cu includes the CSR5 headers but I found no cuSPARSE or merge-SpMV comparison output in it, so the repo itself does not reproduce a comparison. Context: the DASP paper (SC'23, same lab) reports DASP beating TileSpMV by 2.09x on average in FP64 on A100 (search-result text only), so TileSpMV is no longer the lab's fastest method. Makefile arch flags are mixed (compute_61 virtual arch with sm_86 code).

name: AmgT (tensor-core AMG)
workload: Algebraic multigrid solves on SuiteSparse matrices where AmgT replaces HYPRE's SpGEMM (setup phase) and SpMV (solve phase) with tensor-core kernels over a new mBSR storage format, in FP64 and mixed precision; the repo builds three executables (AmgT_FP64, AmgT_Mixed, and cuSPARSE = HYPRE baseline).
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'24): AmgT outperforms the original GPU version of HYPRE by a factor of on geomean 1.46x, 1.32x and 2.24x (up to 2.10x, 2.06x and 3.67x) on NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 GPUs, respectively. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text; which phase or total time they cover is not stated there.)
compiler_and_flags: compile.sh: CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.0; HYPRE configured with --with-cuda --enable-unified-memory and --with-gpu-arch='80 80' (A100) or '90 90' (H100); -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80 (or compute_90); README advises CUDA 12.2+ and OpenMPI 4.0+. No explicit CXX optimization flags are visible in compile.sh.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 (per the paper text returned by search); repo recommends compute capability 8.0; host CPU not verified
tradeoffs: Implemented inside a modified copy of HYPRE (AmgT_HYPRE/), not a standalone library: using it means taking that fork or porting the mBSR data structure (seq_mv.h), SpGEMM (csr_spgemm_device.c) and SpMV (csr_matvec_device.c). The variant is chosen at build time by copying config_files/<variant>.h over seq_mv.h. Needs tensor-core GPUs (compute capability 8.0 or newer) for the main gains; the mixed-precision mode changes numerics. The embedded HYPRE code carries its own license files, which I did not inspect.
caveats: The paper could not be opened (dl.acm.org, ieeexplore, ssslab.cn are egress-blocked); the benchmark_url was returned by WebSearch and the numbers come from that result's abstract-level text ('snippet only'). The repo README has no numbers and the repo has no result tables, but it does contain the HYPRE+cuSPARSE baseline executable, so the HYPRE comparison is reproducible from repo code; no AmgX comparison was found. Hardware CPU model, HYPRE version and per-matrix problem set were not verified, so B rather than A. The 2.24x on MI210 comes from a different GPU vendor path than the tensor-core story. FP64 versus mixed-precision split of the quoted geomeans is not stated in the snippet. Not a GitHub fork, so is_fork_of is null even though it embeds modified HYPRE.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/AmgT and one WebSearch query for the SC'24 paper numbers

name: Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM (KKSPGEMM / KKMEM)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpGEMM (CUDA 8.0.44) on P100; Intel MKL sparse-sparse multiply (MKL-INS, MKL7, MKL8 variants; intel-18.0.128) on Knights Landing
workload: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (symbolic plus numeric phases, 'NoReuse' case) on 81-83 SuiteSparse/UFL multiplications (mostly A*A); best time over thread counts per method; Kokkos 2.50 / Kokkos Kernels 2.60; the wiki ties the setup to the Deveci et al. paper 'Multi-threaded Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication for Many-Core and GPU Architectures'.
claimed_speedup: All figures derived from page data (I parsed the xlsx tables linked from the SpGEMM_Benchmarks wiki page, skipping their summary rows; ratio = baseline time / KKSPGEMM time per matrix, then geometric mean over matrices where both ran). P100: KKSPGEMM faster than cuSPARSE on 75 of 81 multiplications, geomean 3.61x (the table's own geomean row shows 0.441 s vs 0.122 s); faster than viennaCL CUDA on 62 of 72, geomean 1.95x; but NOT faster than Nsparse (faster on only 28 of 77, geomean ratio 0.92x). KNL flat-DDR: versus MKL-INS 1.25x (faster on 63 of 83), MKL7 1.79x (75 of 83), MKL8 2.95x (72 of 78). KNL cache mode: MKL-INS 1.19x (56 of 83), MKL7 2.25x (80 of 83), MKL8 3.75x (77 of 78). Power8 OpenMP versus viennaCL: 2.79x (78 of 83).
compiler_and_flags: P100 runs: nvcc_wrapper (CUDA 8.0.44) with gcc 5.4.0, CXXFLAGS='-Wall -pedantic -Werror -O3 -g -Wshadow -Wsign-compare -Wignored-qualifiers -Wempty-body -Wclobbered -Wuninitialized', KOKKOS_ARCHS=Pascal60,Power8, cuSPARSE TPL, eti-only, double/int; KNL runs: icpc (Intel 18.2.199) with the same flags, KOKKOS_ARCHS=KNL, MKL TPL; OMP_PROC_BIND=spread, OMP_PLACES=threads; first run discarded as warm-up, 6 runs.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla P100-SXM2-16GB (host Power8, machine 'White'); Intel Knights Landing 68-core nodes (machine 'Bowman', up to 256 threads, quadrant mode); Power8 for the viennaCL comparison. Exact CPU SKUs not stated.
tradeoffs: Templated C++ on top of Kokkos (needs the Kokkos library, explicit template instantiation 'eti-only' builds); one source targets OpenMP, CUDA and other Kokkos backends instead of hand-tuned vendor code. Also wraps cuSPARSE, MKL, cuBLAS and MAGMA as optional TPLs. Covers BLAS, sparse BLAS, graph (coloring, triangle counting), Gauss-Seidel and batched kernels. Performance depends on the Kokkos backend and architecture flags chosen at build time.
caveats: Results are from 2018 (Kokkos 2.50, CUDA 8, KNL and P100 hardware, MKL 18.0, cuSPARSE of that CUDA); modern cuSPARSE/MKL SpGEMM may differ. On P100 KKSPGEMM is on average slower than Nsparse (v1.2), so it is not the fastest GPU SpGEMM there. None of the baselines is in the catalog's listed set (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), and the wiki's SpMV benchmark page compares only against Kokkos Kernels' own reference implementation, so SpMV carries no incumbent comparison. Per-matrix times are best over thread counts. CPU SKU is not given (only architecture names), so a strict reading of 'hardware stated' would give B. The wiki is marked deprecated (new docs on kokkos.org, which I could not open); xlsx tables used: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/kokkos/kokkos-kernels/figures/spgemm_benchmark/P100-table.xlsx and .../knl-ddr-table.xlsx, .../knl-cache-table.xlsx, .../power8-table.xlsx; setup page https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/kokkos/kokkos-kernels/p100_configure.md. The tables also contain their own geomean summary rows, which I excluded from my paired ratios; the P100 sheet is oddly named 'Power8' inside the xlsx but its columns are the P100 runs.

name: SPRAL SSIDS
language: Fortran (with C interface; GPU build via CUDA)
baseline: HSL_MA97, MUMPS, PARDISO (named by the task lead only; the paper's actual baselines could not be verified)
workload: Sparse symmetric indefinite LDL^T direct solves on CPU, multi-GPU and heterogeneous nodes; the README cites Hogg, Ovtchinnikov and Scott, ACM TOMS 42(1), 2016 for SSIDS.
claimed_speedup: No numbers found. The repo README, docs/Fortran/ssids.rst, ChangeLog and repo listing contain no performance comparison against MA97, MUMPS, PARDISO or any other solver.
tradeoffs: Needs METIS and hwloc (hwloc built with CUDA support for GPU use) and a BLAS/LAPACK; builds with Meson. Environment variables OMP_CANCELLATION=TRUE and OMP_PROC_BIND=TRUE must be set or SSIDS fails with error flag -53. Per its docs the solve phase is performed in serial at present. Does posdef Cholesky or indefinite factorization with 1x1 and 2x2 pivots; leaf subtrees are pre-assigned to NUMA regions or GPUs.
caveats: Evidence not reachable: the SSIDS GPU paper (TOMS 2016; preprint RAL-P-2014-006 on epubs.stfc.ac.uk) and the CPU a-posteriori-pivoting report cited in the docs are on egress-blocked hosts (epubs.stfc.ac.uk, numerical.rl.ac.uk, doi.org), and my WebSearch budget was spent on other projects, so no baseline names or ratios are verified. A verifier with access to the TOMS paper could probably re-tier to B (peer reviewed, hardware described in the paper, comparison against HSL codes). The baselines named in the task lead are not in the catalog's list for this category (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), so baseline_in_list is false. The ChangeLog entry of 2016-09-23 says SSIDS v2 added CPU, multi-GPU and heterogeneous execution.
